title: NoSQL systems
lead: Scaling through sharding and replication, CAP, BASE and NoSQL data models.

sections.title: Motivation, sharding and replication
sections.html:
Workload motivation, sharding and replication

Large web applications can have fast-growing unpredictable OLTP traffic. Coordinating cross-node transactions and synchronising replicas can be expensive. Sharding distributes ownership and capacity: a single-shard write can be local, but multi-shard reads/transactions need routing and coordination. Sharding does not intrinsically require locks for every read; that depends on the concurrency protocol.

Replication supplies extra copies for read distribution and fault tolerance. A write must be propagated according to the consistency policy, either synchronously or asynchronously; slow propagation can yield stale reads. More copies do not make every write cheaper or every failure harmless. These workload pressures motivate alternative models and trade-offs.

PDF pp. 1–4

Not Only SQL and the role of restricted operations

NoSQL is a family of systems, not one consistency contract. Flexible fields, simpler access models and restricted operations can make horizontal partitioning easier. Flexibility can defer or relocate schema enforcement rather than eliminate all structure. The source popularity chart is historical context, not evidence of performance or suitability.

The ACID recap remains relevant: atomicity, invariant consistency, isolation and durability are distinct. Some NoSQL systems support transactions, and some relational deployments scale horizontally. The source’s broad contrast introduces common design motivations; it is not a theorem that the label determines capabilities.

PDF pp. 5–8

sections.title: CAP theorem
sections.html:
CAP precisely, including the source simplifications

CAP’s consistency is a single-copy/linearizable view: completed operations appear to take effect in a real-time-respecting order. It is different from ACID consistency, which concerns invariants. Availability in the theorem requires a successful response satisfying the operation’s specification from a non-failing node; an arbitrary error response does not satisfy it. This corrects the slide’s overly broad “success or failure” wording.

During a network partition, two sides cannot communicate. If both accept operations without coordination, a read can miss a write completed on the other side, violating linearizability. To preserve that consistency, some operations must wait or be rejected, sacrificing theorem availability. Thus “pick any two at any moment” is an imprecise mnemonic: the conflict is C versus A during a partition under the theorem’s model. The source’s taxonomy picture is an illustration, not a permanent guarantee for every configuration of a product.

PDF pp. 9–10

sections.title: BASE and key-value/column-family models
sections.html:
BASE and eventual convergence

BASE abbreviates Basically Available, Soft State, Eventually Consistent. A replica can answer with stale data; background propagation can change its state without a new client write. Eventual consistency promises convergence under the specified assumptions, typically after writes stop and updates can be delivered and reconciled. It provides no universal time bound and does not by itself guarantee read-your-writes, monotonic reads or conflict resolution quality. “Basically available” is a design description, not a proof that every request survives every failure.

PDF p. 11

Four model families

Key–value stores expose unique keys and opaque values for caches, sessions and direct retrieval. Document stores expose structured fields for profiles/content/catalogues. Column-family or wide-column stores organise sparse records around row keys and column families; this model is not the same as the analytical columnar layout in lecture 7. Graph databases model vertices, edges and often properties for relationships and traversal. The product examples in the slide illustrate families, not a universal feature or performance ranking.

PDF pp. 12–13

Key–value operations and replica staleness

The abstract interface has get(key),put(key,value),del(key). Examples are user:42→a profile object, session:xyz→logged_in and counter:views→1048576. In this simple model the engine does not query inside the value, although real products can add richer operations.

Hashing assigns key k to h(k); replication can place copies at h1(k),h2(k),h3(k). After put at one copy, an immediate get from a copy not yet updated may return the old value. An application needing read-your-writes must use an appropriate routing/session/consistency mechanism; merely choosing a unique key does not solve stale reads.

PDF p. 14

sections.title: Documents and semi-structured data
sections.html:
Structured documents and JSON

Instead of storing an opaque list of all flights on a date, expose the value’s internal structure. Document queries can inspect nested fields; the source example db.users.find({age: {$gt: 25}}) filters users by age. Documents can use JSON/BSON or other structured representations depending on the system.

JSON objects contain named members; arrays are ordered sequences; values include strings, numbers, booleans, null, objects and arrays. A collection can contain documents with different fields, but indexes, validation rules and application expectations still create structure. A missing field and a field explicitly set to null need not have identical query behaviour.

PDF pp. 15–16

Relational and nested models

The source contrasts flat tables with nested document trees, explicit table schemas with flexible documents, and relational joins with document-oriented queries. Treat binary-versus-text and “avoids joins” as simplified comparisons: JSON is an exchange syntax, engines can store binary documents, relational systems can store/query JSON, and document products can support joins or validation. Choose representation and operations separately from a marketing label.

PDF p. 17

sections.title: Graphs and workload-driven choice
sections.html:
Property graphs and pattern queries

Graph nodes represent entities, directed edges represent relationships, and properties annotate either. Queries include fixed patterns, friends-of-friends traversals, reachability and shortest/variable-length paths. Expressiveness and path semantics depend on the language and engine.

The source asks for cars driven by Dan. Its Cypher example is:

MATCH (:Person {name: "Dan"})-[:DRIVES]->(car)
RETURN car;

The pattern binds the destination car of an outgoing DRIVES edge from a Person named Dan; reversing the arrow asks a different relationship. GQL and SQL/PGQ address property graphs; Cypher is another property-graph language; SPARQL targets RDF graphs. Their names do not make their syntax or graph models interchangeable.

PDF pp. 18–19

Popularity versus choosing a system

The ranking slide combines mentions, searches, jobs and social signals; it is not a workload benchmark. The closing SQL/NoSQL table suggests considering transactions, joins, evolving schemas, write throughput and horizontal scaling, then explicitly notes the boundary is blurring.

Specify required invariants, transaction scope, query patterns, latency under load and allowed stale-read/failure behaviour. Compare concrete configurations against those requirements. Relational JSON, transactional document stores and distributed SQL show why neither “SQL” nor “NoSQL” alone answers the engineering choice. The lecture ends with workload-based trade-offs, not a claim that one family replaces the other.

PDF pp. 20–21

quiz.question: Two replicas cannot communicate, and one has acknowledged a new write. What is the problem if a later read at the other replica immediately returns the old value?
options: It does not preserve linearizable consistency.
It cannot be a NoSQL system.
quiz.explanation: A read that starts after a successful write but returns the old value does not satisfy linearizability. This is the central trade-off illustrated by CAP.

source.summary: Lecture 27 covers the motivation for NoSQL, sharding and replication, CAP and BASE, data models, and workload-driven choices. This learning material also explains how to interpret simplified CAP diagrams carefully.
